en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the yoke of the tradition of the venerable teacher Prabhākara.
Adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and the gloss on difficult passages (*viṣamasthala-ṭippaṇī*), it is named *Amṛtakalā*.
The Fifth Chapter: 81. The Definition of Valid Cognition (pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa).
82. Direct experience (anubhūti) is valid cognition; it is distinct from memory, whereas memory is [not].
Knowledge arising solely from the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior cognition is called recollection. // 1 //
Memory is not a means of valid cognition because it depends upon a prior apprehension; however, successive cognitions in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhika-buddhi) are independent of one another.
The collection of means of valid cognition accepted by Prabhākara is as follows:
"In that regard, there are five kinds of knowledge: perception, inference, likewise scripture, comparison, and presumptive testimony—this is the opinion of the Sage. (3)
The Definition of Perception:

Direct cognition is perception; it [applies] to the object of knowledge (meya), the knower (mātṛ), and the means of knowledge (pramā). Regarding objects of knowledge, it arises from the contact of the sense organs with substances, universals, and qualities. (4)
Perceptual cognition is held to be both conceptual and non-conceptual;
the former has a qualified object as its domain, while the other has its own intrinsic nature as its domain. (5)

All valid cognition (pramā) arises from the causes of all consciousness; because it possesses the common quality of being a direct knower, it is recognized as perception (pratyakṣa) with respect to both the object of measurement (miti) and the subject who measures (mātṛ). // 6 //

An Examination of the Nature of the Means of Valid Cognition and its Result: The validity of cognitions consists in their external [correspondence], while the result is [the capacity for] rejection, acquisition, and so forth;
however, for knowledge itself, the result is that very [cognition] which is serviceable for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). (7)

And the instrument is relative—whether it be the mind, the sense organ itself, or the contact between that [organ] and its object; if this is the means of knowledge, then the preceding [contact] is the result.
The Definition of Inference:

Inference is the cognition of another part [of a known relation] arising from the perception of one part, when the rule of the connection between them is already known, provided it is not sublated. (9)

Whatever relation exists here between one thing and another that is unconditional and established by means of valid cognition such as perception—that [relation] is considered the indicator of that [related object]. (10)

The object of inference—consisting of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) whether perceived or unperceived—and the statement along with its refutations, have been described by implication through this [work].
Just as in the case of perception, the description of the means of knowledge and its result should also be stated here. 12.
Definition of Scripture:
Scripture, however, is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of words. (13)
The examination of analogy (*upamāna*).

Analogy is a cognition arising from the perception of similarity, which has similarity as its object. Its object is established by that cognition as distinct from the categories of substance and the rest. 14.
That cognition which, arising with respect to a correlate (pratiyogin) from something perceived due to similarity, has similarity as its object, is called comparison (upamāna). // 15 //

The Determination of Presumption (Arthāpatti): That conceptualization which leads a perceived object to a state of impossibility without another perceived object—[that] is presumption (arthāpatti). (16)

Just as existence within the house is established by means of non-existence [therein] without the conceptualization of [existence] outside, so too, when [existence] outside is being postulated, its impossibility must be understood in the same way.

In this context, the impossibility of the object to be known—characterized by the occurrence of doubt due to contradiction with other means of valid cognition—is established without recourse to conceptual construction. (18)
For a state of non-occurrence apart from a specific location is never observed;
therefore, even if [the reason] is established by way of non-occurrence, it falls into doubt because of that [location]. (19)

The conceptual construction that proceeds for the purpose of dispelling that doubt is known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because it arises from an object that itself gives rise to doubt. (20)
When an object, though perceived, falls into doubt unless a certain conceptualization is applied, some declare that presumption (*arthāpatti*) consists precisely in that conceptualization. (21)

In inference, however, the indicator (gamaka) is characterized by its absence from the counter-example (vipakṣa); thus, its impossibility [in the counter-example] is understood without the object to be inferred (gamya). (22)

It is certain that these two means of valid cognition, known as presumption (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*), are distinct from one another due to the difference in their respective causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). // 23 //
The Refutation of Non-apprehension as a Means of Valid Cognition:
This rebuttal is now stated by the Prābhākaras against those wise ones who assert that non-existence (abhāva) is a sixth means of valid cognition. (24)
Indeed, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which brings about the comprehension of some object of cognition (prameya).
In this regard, let it first be considered: what is the object of cognition for non-existence (abhāva)? (25)
But surely, that which is conceived as an object of cognition by the thought "it does not exist" will be the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (abhāva). // 26 //
The cognition that arises here, "there is no jar on this ground," would not pertain to the bare ground alone, because it would then apply even where a jar is present. (27)
If it were to exist on the bare ground alone, what kind of isolation (kaivalya) would that be?
It is not merely its own nature; otherwise, it would have to be called a different property (dharmāntara). (28)
In this case, another object of cognition (prameya) would necessarily have to be admitted;
and that [object] cannot be known by the senses, because it does not depend upon their operation. // 29 //
Even when an entity is perceived merely in its own form, one who has traveled far away and has somehow developed a desire to know it does not conclude that it is non-existent. (30)

Therefore, even where one with functioning sense faculties perceives non-existence, the status of perception as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies there too, but only with respect to the aspect of existence. (31)
The non-existence of the means of valid cognition is understood precisely through their non-arising;
for indeed, there is no apprehension of non-existence anywhere without that [non-arising]. (32)
Because the non-arising of a valid cognition capable [of apprehending it] is accepted as the cause [of non-perception],
even the fault of over-extension finds no opportunity.
And non-arising, when it is not known, cannot be a cause like the sense organs;
therefore, even the suspicion that it might function as a logical mark is refuted from afar. (34)
If non-arising were known by means of a cause, it would be like a logical mark (liṅga);
this would lead to an infinite regress, and its non-existence could not be established. // 35 //
Furthermore, activities such as walking upon the ground do not proceed by means of the mere delimitation of the ground alone. (36)
In that case, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would be unavoidable, for [the cognition] would arise even with respect to a spot of ground possessed of thorns and the like;
or else, it proceeds from the delimitation of a portion of the earth as such [in its isolation]. (37)
In that case, is absolute isolation (kaivalya) to be conceptualized as belonging to the object of apprehension or to the act of apprehension?
If it belongs to the object of apprehension, then the fault already mentioned previously would necessarily follow.
If that were the case for the planet, then the desire for subtle knowledge would be fruitless;
for it is consciousness alone that has arisen as the cause of worldly transaction. // 39 //

Therefore, having delimited an entity, when one desires to engage in conventional discourse, subtle investigation is appropriate for the purpose of establishing whether it is perceived or not perceived. (40)
To this it is replied: there are two types of cognition regarding an object such as the ground;
one has a composite object as its domain, while the other has that [simple] element alone as its domain. (41)
That [non-apprehension] which has only that [object] as its object is also twofold:
it occurs when the counter-correlative is invisible, and when the counter-correlative is visible. (42)

In that regard, this cognition of "mere-that" (tanmātra) with respect to the perceptible object serves as the counter-correlate; it is that very cognition which constitutes the non-existence of a counter-correlate such as a jar on a patch of ground. (43)
But surely, how could there arise a cognition of that alone regarding something which was previously determined by a cognition of a mixture, if that [mixture] were not present there? (44)
It can be said that even in the absence of that [effect], "how could there be an absence of that which was present there?"— if one were to ask this, the reason for it must be stated.
Therefore, it is better that the cause of that [cognition] be simply the cognition of the subtle elements (tanmātra), because that is accepted by both disputants alike. (46)

Non-perception is not a cause [of knowledge] when it is unexamined, like the eye; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the state of one who has fallen asleep would be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). // 47 //
Visibility does not serve as a differentiator for that negation;
for a positive characteristic cannot logically belong to a non-entity.
Even when non-perception has ceased, people still designate the prior non-existence of something that was never previously seen. (49)
By that [non-perception], the non-perception of the visible is known; yet that which is existent is not made known by it.
If its knowledge were [derived] from the non-perception of the visible, there would be an infinite regress.
If that [cognition] were of the nature of the awareness of itself alone, then there would be no perception [of an object];
in that case, the infinite regress regarding its self-awareness would cease.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that non-perception has as its object the visible domain; for non-existence is essentially the experience of that [domain] alone. (52)
This experience of the mere locus (tanmātra), which is characterized by non-perception, when reflected upon in relation to the ground and so forth, is designated as the absence of that [object]. (53)
Furthermore, this experience of the subtle elements (tanmātra) is not an object of cognition because it exists as the result [of cognition];
moreover, those learned in logic know that this [experience] is self-luminous.
The word "it does not exist" applies only to that which is self-cognized;
therefore, it does not coincide with the logical principle of the cognition "it does not exist. (55)
In the absence of the object, how could there be a means of cognition called "non-existence"?
For neither the existence nor the non-existence of a jar can be apprehended through the aforementioned sequence.
For the conventional usage regarding non-existence—such as walking about without hesitation and so forth—proceeds solely through the aforementioned experience of that [absence] alone. (57)
When there is non-perception of something despite its being perceptible, then the conventional usage of its non-existence proceeds. // 58 //
Thus, even the desire to know subtle thorns has attained its purpose;
for without that [desire], the state of being visible does not apply to the existence of the subtle. (59)
Furthermore, the engagement in worldly transaction is based upon the perception and non-perception of what is observable;
therefore, it is logical to examine that [subject] for the sake of establishing its observability. (60)
If that is so, what then is the meaning of this treatise on definitions?
Let the nectar of the doctrine, produced from the ocean of Mīmāṃsā, be drunk! // 61 //

Those who assert that there is a means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (abhāva) which establishes a fourfold object of knowledge known as non-existence, [an object] that cannot be determined by perception and the other [means of knowledge], [are the opponents]. (62)
This effort was undertaken by the author of the Bhāṣya for the purpose of refuting that [view]:
that the non-existence of something not in contact [with the senses] is what makes known the cognition "it does not exist. (63)
The absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva) is said to be the case when something does not constitute a means of valid cognition.
If it is thought: "What, then, is the result of this negation here? (64)
It is said: the treatise on definitions establishes perception and the other means of knowledge; for it is certain that in all cases, a means of knowledge is understood through its effect. (65)
It is also agreed that the function of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is ascertainment;
and ascertainment is the cognition that "this is precisely this" regarding all things. (66)
And that [non-apprehension] occurs when there is a cognition of the absence of another object;
it is the non-arising of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in a place where an absence is determined. (67)

In that case, the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge would exist simultaneously with it; and it is only for such a [simultaneous] entity that a definition being formulated is appropriate. (68)
It was not done by him in that manner, nor were the characteristics of a virtuous person performed;
in order to dispel this doubt, the refutation is now stated. (69)
But how is this doubt, which has been refuted here, [still] present, such that it must be sought out again with the claim that "there is no object of cognition called non-existence"? (70)
"The non-arising of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) has been correctly established as their defining characteristic"; thus he summarizes the definitions of the aforementioned pramāṇas. (71)
The author of the Bhāṣya composed this treatise; it does not have non-existence as its defining characteristic.
[Objection: Even so, why did he speak of "five" while omitting the word "sound"? (72)
The author of the Commentary, while resolving the objections raised against the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), states:
"[They are taught] for the sake of establishing that which serves as the cause for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). (73)
Thus it is said: even conventional reality, though possessing a dual nature, is established;
therein, the conventional designation of existence is found only within the five [aggregates]. (74)

The conventional usage of "non-existence," however, arises from the reflective awareness of not seeing what is perceptible; for that [awareness] is bound by the delimitation of the mere presence of the location of the ground. (75)

That the conventional usage of "absence" [is established] has already been demonstrated previously, in this ocean of Mīmāṃsā, which is its own natural locus for testing all the jewels of method without exception. (76)
Thus the wise Śālikanātha has extracted this drop of nectar.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Drop of Nectar" (*Amṛtakalā*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor, the venerable Śālikanātha Miśra.
